title: Book VI: The Widow And The Wife — Chapter LXI
paragraphs:
“Inconsistencies,” answered Imlac, “cannot both be right, but imputed
to man they may both be true.”—_Rasselas_.
That same night, Mr. Bulstrode came home from a business trip to Brassing. His good wife met him in the hall and led him into his private sitting room.
“Nicholas,” she said, her honest eyes fixed anxiously on his, “such an unpleasant man came here asking for you. He’s left me quite upset.”
“What sort of man, my dear?” Mr. Bulstrode asked, already horribly certain of the answer.

“A red-faced man with big whiskers and the most insolent manners. He insisted he was an old friend and said you’d be sorry to miss him. He wanted to wait here, but I told him he could see you at the Bank tomorrow morning. So insolent! He stared at me and said his friend Nick had been lucky in his wives. I don’t believe he would have left at all if Blucher hadn’t broken his chain and come running round on the gravel. I was in the garden, you see, so I said, ‘You’d better leave. The dog’s very fierce, and I can’t hold him.’ Do you really know anything about a man like that?”

“I think I know who it is, my dear,” Mr. Bulstrode replied in his usual quiet voice. “An unfortunate, dissolute creature I helped too generously years ago. Still, I expect he won’t trouble you again. He’ll probably come to the Bank—begging, no doubt.”

They said nothing more about it until the following day, when Mr. Bulstrode had come back from town and was dressing for dinner. Unsure whether he was home, his wife looked into his dressing room. He had taken off his coat and cravat and stood with one arm resting on a chest of drawers, staring blankly at the floor. He gave a nervous start and looked up when she came in.
“Nicholas, you look terribly ill. Is something wrong?”
“My head is very painful,” said Mr. Bulstrode. He suffered so often from poor health that his wife was always willing to accept it as the reason for his low spirits.
“Sit down. Let me bathe it with vinegar.”

His body had no need of the vinegar, but her loving attention comforted his spirit. Though invariably polite, he generally accepted such care with the coolness of a husband receiving what was due to him. Today, however, as she bent over him, he said, “You’re very good to me, Harriet.” Something in his voice was new to her. She could not have said what it was, but her concern flashed into the thought that he might be about to fall seriously ill.
“Has something upset you?” she asked. “Did that man come to the Bank?”
“Yes. It was just as I expected. He once had the chance to make something better of himself, but he’s fallen into drunkenness and debauchery.”

“Has he gone away for good?” Mrs. Bulstrode asked anxiously. She stopped herself, for particular reasons, from adding, “It was very unpleasant to hear him claiming to be your friend.” Just then she did not want to suggest her customary awareness that her husband’s early connections were not quite the equal of her own. She knew little about them. He had first worked in a bank, then gone into what he called business in the City and made a fortune before he was thirty-three. He had married a widow much older than himself, a Dissenter, and probably inferior in various other ways of the sort a second wife, judging impartially, can usually discover in a first. Beyond this she had scarcely cared to inquire. His stories sometimes offered glimpses of his early religious interests, his wish to become a preacher, and his involvement in missionary and charitable work. She believed him an excellent man. His piety seemed particularly distinguished in someone who was not a clergyman; his influence had made her own outlook more serious; and his worldly possessions had raised her position. Yet she also liked to think that winning Harriet Vincy’s hand had benefited him in every respect. Her family’s standing was beyond question by Middlemarch standards, which surely cast a better light on things than any London street or dissenting chapel yard. The old provincial outlook distrusted London. And though true religion could save souls anywhere, honest Mrs. Bulstrode felt sure that salvation within the established Church was more respectable. She was so eager for others to overlook her husband’s former life as a London Dissenter that she liked to avoid the subject even with him. He knew this perfectly well. In some ways he was rather afraid of his candid wife, whose borrowed piety and inborn worldliness were equally sincere. She had nothing to be ashamed of, and he had married her from a real affection that still endured. His fears, however, were those of a man concerned to preserve his acknowledged superiority. To lose his wife’s high opinion—or anyone else’s, unless they plainly hated him as an enemy of religious truth—would feel like the beginning of death. When she asked—
“Has he gone away for good?”
“Oh, I trust he has,” he replied, trying to sound as calmly unconcerned as possible!

In reality, Mr. Bulstrode was nowhere near a state of peaceful trust. During their interview at the Bank, Raffles had made it clear that his appetite for torment was almost as strong as his other appetites. He freely admitted he had made a detour to Middlemarch simply to look around and see whether it might suit him as a place to live. He had, certainly, found more debts waiting than he had expected, but he had not spent the whole two hundred pounds. A mere twenty-five would be enough to send him on his way for now. His chief desire had been to see his friend Nick and the family, and learn everything about the good fortune of someone so dear to him. Later he might come back for a longer visit. This time he refused to be “escorted off the premises,” as he put it: he would not leave Middlemarch under Bulstrode’s supervision. He meant to take the coach the next day—if he felt like it.

Bulstrode knew he was powerless. Threats and persuasion were equally useless. He could rely neither on a lasting fear nor on a promise. Instead, his heart held the cold conviction that unless Providence intervened by sending death, Raffles would soon be back in Middlemarch. That certainty terrified him.

He was not facing prosecution or destitution. The only danger was that certain facts from his past would be exposed to his neighbors’ judgment and his wife’s sorrowful understanding. Those facts would make him an object of contempt and disgrace the religion with which he had so carefully identified himself. Fear of judgment sharpens the memory. It throws an inescapable light over the long-neglected past we have been accustomed to recall only in vague phrases. Even without memory, our life’s growth and decline form a continuous chain of dependence; but vivid memory compels a man to acknowledge a blameworthy past as his own. When remembrance stings like a reopened wound, that past is no dead history, no discarded preparation for the present, no repented error shaken free of one’s life. It is a living, trembling part of oneself, sending back shudders, bitter tastes, and the prickling heat of deserved shame.

Bulstrode’s past had now returned to this second kind of life; only its pleasures seemed to have lost their force. Day and night, except for short spells of sleep that merely wove memory and fear into a fantastic present, the scenes of his earlier life stood between him and everything else. They persisted like the reflections that face us when we look out of a lighted room: instead of grass and trees, we see the objects behind our backs. The sequence of inner and outward events appeared all at once. He might dwell on each in turn, but the others never loosened their grip on his awareness.

He saw himself again as the young bank clerk: pleasant-looking, as good with figures as he was fluent in speech, and fond of defining points of theology. Though young, he had been a leading member of a Calvinist dissenting congregation in Highbury, with powerful experiences of sin and forgiveness to describe. Once again he heard himself called upon as Brother Bulstrode at prayer meetings, speaking from religious platforms and preaching in private houses. He remembered considering the ministry as a possible calling and feeling drawn to missionary work. Those had been his happiest days. That was the point in his life at which he would now have chosen to wake and discover that everything since had been a dream. The circle in which Brother Bulstrode stood out was small, but its members were close to him, and that closeness deepened his satisfaction. His power extended over little ground, yet he felt its effect all the more intensely. He found it easy to believe that grace had worked exceptionally within him and that the signs marked him out as a special instrument of God.

Then came the turning point. An orphan educated at a charitable commercial school, he had felt himself promoted when Mr. Dunkirk, the wealthiest member of the congregation, invited him to his fine villa. Soon he was a familiar guest. The wife honored his piety; the husband recognized his ability. Dunkirk’s fortune came from a flourishing trade in the City and the West End. This redirected Bulstrode’s ambition. His future usefulness to God now seemed to lie in combining outstanding religious gifts with success in business.

In time there came what looked like a clear outward direction. A trusted junior partner died, leaving a vacancy the principal keenly felt. He could imagine no one better suited to fill it than his young friend Bulstrode, if Bulstrode would agree to become his confidential accountant. Bulstrode accepted. It was a pawnbroking business, magnificent in both its scale and its profits. Before long he discovered that one source of those magnificent profits was a willingness to accept any goods offered without asking searching questions about where they came from. But the firm had a West End branch, and nothing shabby or small about it suggested that one should feel ashamed.

He remembered his first recoil. It took place in private and was accompanied by arguments, some of which took the form of prayer. The business was established, with roots stretching far back. Surely opening a new gin palace was one thing and accepting an investment in an existing one another? Where, in human dealings, could anyone draw the boundary at which profits made from lost souls began? Wasn’t this even God’s method of saving His chosen? “You know,” the young Bulstrode had said, just as the older man was saying now, “you know how little my soul is attached to these things. I see them only as tools for cultivating your garden, reclaimed here and there from the wilderness.”

He had plenty of metaphors and precedents, and no shortage of special spiritual experiences. Eventually these made staying in his position seem a service required of him. The prospect of a fortune had already opened before him, and his misgivings remained private. Mr. Dunkirk had never expected misgivings at all: he had never imagined that trade had anything to do with the plan of salvation. Bulstrode did, in fact, lead two separate lives. His religious work could not conflict with his business once he had reasoned himself out of feeling any conflict.

Now, surrounded again in thought by that past, he offered the same defenses. Indeed, over the years he had kept spinning them into denser and more tangled webs that cushioned his moral sense. As age made his self-interest more eager while giving him less enjoyment, his soul had grown still more steeped in the conviction that he did everything for God’s sake and cared nothing for himself. Yet if he could return to that distant time, with all the poverty of his youth, he would choose to be a missionary.

But the chain of causes into which he had fastened himself continued. Trouble came to the fine villa at Highbury. Years earlier, the only daughter had run away, defied her parents, and gone on the stage. Now the only son died, and shortly afterward Mr. Dunkirk died too. His wife, a simple, devout woman, was left with all the wealth both inside and outside that magnificent business, whose exact nature she had never understood. She had come to trust Bulstrode and to adore him innocently, as women often adore their priest or their minister appointed by men. It was natural that, after a while, they should think of marriage. But Mrs. Dunkirk felt troubled longings for her daughter, who had long been treated as lost to both God and her parents. They knew the daughter had married, but she had vanished completely. Having lost her boy, the mother pictured a grandson and wanted to reclaim her daughter in both senses of the word. If the daughter were found, some of the wealth—perhaps a large share—would go toward providing for several grandchildren. Before Mrs. Dunkirk would marry again, they must try to find her. Bulstrode agreed. But after advertisements and other inquiries failed, the mother believed her daughter could not be found and consented to marry without setting any property aside.
The daughter had been found. Only one man besides Bulstrode knew it, and he had been paid to keep quiet and go away.

That was the naked fact Bulstrode was now forced to confront, with the hard outline an action presents to an outsider. To him at the time, and even now in his burning memory, it had been divided into little steps. Each step had been justified as he took it by arguments that seemed to establish its righteousness. He believed remarkable acts of Providence had sanctioned his course up to then. They seemed to point toward his becoming the agent who would put a large fortune to its best use and rescue it from misuse. Death, and other striking arrangements such as a woman’s trusting nature, had intervened. Bulstrode would have echoed Cromwell: “Do you call these mere events? May the Lord pity you!” The events were relatively small, but the essential condition was present: they favored his own purposes. He could easily decide what he owed others by asking what God intended for him. Would God’s service benefit if a considerable part of this fortune went to a young woman and her husband devoted to frivolous pursuits, who might squander it on trivial things? Such people seemed outside the course of special providence. Bulstrode had never told himself in advance, “The daughter must not be found.” Nevertheless, when the moment came, he concealed her existence. Later, he comforted the mother with the thought that the unhappy young woman was probably dead.

There were times when he felt he had acted wrongly, but how could he turn back? He performed spiritual exercises, called himself nothing, held fast to redemption, and continued serving as God’s instrument. Five years later, Death widened his path again by taking his wife. He gradually withdrew his capital, but he did not make the sacrifices necessary to close the business. It continued another thirteen years before finally collapsing. Meanwhile, Nicholas Bulstrode had used his hundred thousand pounds prudently and become a solidly important figure in the provinces: a banker, a member of the Church, a public benefactor. He was also a silent partner in businesses where he applied his skill to reducing the cost of raw materials, as with the dyes that rotted Mr. Vincy’s silk. Now, after almost thirty undisturbed years of respectability, during which everything earlier had lain numb in his awareness, that past had risen and flooded his mind. It was as though some terrible new sense had broken into existence and overwhelmed his frail being.

Meanwhile, his conversation with Raffles had taught him something momentous. It became an active force in the struggle between his desires and his fears. Here, he thought, was a possible opening toward spiritual rescue, and perhaps material rescue too.

His need for spiritual rescue was real. Some crude hypocrites may consciously pretend to beliefs and feelings in order to deceive the world, but Bulstrode was not one of them. He was simply a man whose desires had proved stronger than his professed beliefs, and who had gradually explained satisfying those desires until it appeared entirely consistent with those beliefs. If that is hypocrisy, it is a process that occasionally occurs in all of us, whatever our faith. It can happen whether we believe in humanity’s future perfection or in the latest predicted date for the world’s end; whether we consider the earth a rotting nest that preserves a chosen remnant, ourselves included, or passionately believe in human solidarity.

Throughout his life, the service he could render religion had been the reason he gave himself for his actions, the motive he poured into his prayers. Who would make better use of money and position than he intended? Who could surpass him in loathing himself and exalting God’s cause? For Mr. Bulstrode, however, God’s cause was separate from his own upright conduct. It required him to distinguish God’s enemies, to use them only as instruments, and, if possible, to keep money and its accompanying influence out of their hands. Profitable investments in businesses where the prince of this world exercised his most active cunning became holy when God’s servant put their profits to a righteous use.

This unspoken reasoning belongs no more exclusively to evangelical religion than the use of grand phrases to cover petty motives belongs exclusively to Englishmen. Any general doctrine can eat away our morality unless it is checked by a deeply rooted habit of direct sympathy with individual human beings.

Still, someone who believes in something beyond his own greed must have a conscience, some standard to which he adjusts himself more or less. Bulstrode’s standard had been his usefulness to God’s cause. “I am sinful and nothing—a vessel to be made holy through use—but use me!” Into that mold he had forced his enormous need to be important and dominant. Now a moment had come when the mold seemed in danger of shattering and being thrown away altogether.

What if the actions he had accepted because they strengthened him as an instrument of divine glory became an excuse for mockery and a cloud upon that glory? If Providence decreed this, he would be driven out of the temple as a man who had brought impure offerings.

He had long poured out declarations of repentance. Today, however, repentance had a more bitter taste. A threatening Providence was pressing him toward a form of appeasement that involved more than doctrine. The divine court looked different to him now. Humbling himself was no longer enough; he must come with restitution in his hand. It was truly before his God that Bulstrode was preparing to attempt whatever restitution seemed possible. Great dread had taken hold of his sensitive body, and the scorching approach of shame created a new spiritual need. Day and night, as the returning, threatening past formed a conscience within him, he considered how to regain peace and trust, what sacrifice might hold back the rod. In these frightened moments he believed that if he voluntarily did something right, God would spare him the consequences of doing wrong. Religion can change only when the feelings that fill it change; and a religion of personal fear remains close to the level of primitive superstition.

He had watched Raffles actually leave on the Brassing coach, which brought temporary relief. It lifted the pressure of immediate fear but did not end his inward struggle or his need to secure protection. At last he reached a difficult decision and wrote to Will Ladislaw, asking him to come to the Shrubs at nine that evening for a private conversation. Will was not particularly surprised. He supposed the request concerned some new idea about the “Pioneer.” But when he was shown into Mr. Bulstrode’s private room, the banker’s painfully exhausted face struck him. He almost asked, “Are you ill?” Then, checking the abrupt question, he merely asked after Mrs. Bulstrode and whether she was pleased with the picture bought for her.

“Thank you. She’s very pleased. She’s out with our daughters this evening. I asked you here, Mr. Ladislaw, because I have something to tell you of a very private—indeed, I would say sacredly confidential—nature. I imagine nothing could have been further from your thoughts than the existence of important past connections linking your history with mine.”

Will felt something like an electric shock. He was already acutely sensitive about connections with the past, and his agitation had scarcely subsided. His forebodings were unpleasant. It felt like a dream changing shape: the action begun by that loud, bloated stranger was being continued by this sickly figure of respectability with his pale eyes. At that moment the banker’s subdued voice and smooth, formal speech repelled him almost as much as the opposite manner he remembered. His color changed visibly as he answered—
“No. Nothing at all.”

“You see before you, Mr. Ladislaw, a deeply afflicted man. Nothing obliges me to make the disclosure for which I’ve asked you here tonight except the urgency of my conscience and the knowledge that I stand before One who sees differently from man. Under human law, you have no claim on me of any kind.”
Will felt more uneasy than curious. Mr. Bulstrode paused with his head resting on his hand, his eyes on the floor. Then he looked searchingly at Will and said—
“I am told your mother’s name was Sarah Dunkirk and that she left her family to go on the stage. I’m also told your father was once severely wasted by illness. Can you confirm these things?”

“Yes. All of that is true,” Will said. He was struck by the timing of the question: surely such an inquiry should have preceded the banker’s hints. But tonight Mr. Bulstrode had followed the order of his feelings. He had no doubt that the opportunity to make restitution had arrived, and an overwhelming urge drove him to expressions of repentance through which he hoped to avert punishment.
“Do you know anything more about your mother’s family?” he went on.
“No. She didn’t like talking about them. She was an extremely generous and honorable woman,” Will said, almost angrily.
“I don’t mean to accuse her of anything. Did she never say anything at all about her mother?”
“I heard her say she believed her mother didn’t know why she had run away. She used to say ‘poor mother’ in a pitying voice.”

“Her mother became my wife,” said Bulstrode. He paused before continuing. “You have a claim on me, Mr. Ladislaw. As I’ve said, it is not a legal claim, but my conscience acknowledges it. That marriage made me wealthy. This would probably not have happened—certainly not to the same degree—if your grandmother had been able to find her daughter. I understand that daughter is no longer alive!”

“No,” said Will. Suspicion and disgust rose in him so powerfully that, scarcely aware of what he was doing, he picked up his hat from the floor and stood. Everything in him wanted to reject this newly revealed connection.
“Please sit down, Mr. Ladislaw,” Bulstrode said anxiously. “Naturally the sudden discovery has startled you. But I beg you to be patient with someone already weighed down by inward suffering.”
Will sat again. He felt a little pity, half mixed with contempt, at the sight of an elderly man choosing to abase himself.

“Mr. Ladislaw, I want to make up for the loss your mother suffered. I know you have no fortune, and I wish to provide you with an adequate income from wealth that would probably already be yours if your grandmother had known for certain that your mother was alive and could have found her.”

Mr. Bulstrode stopped. He felt that his listener must see this as a striking example of conscientiousness, while God would see an act of repentance. He had no idea what was passing through Will’s mind. Raffles’s unmistakable hints still smarted there, and Will’s natural quickness at putting things together was sharpened by the expectation of discoveries he would gladly have banished back into darkness. For several moments he gave no answer. At the end of his speech Mr. Bulstrode had looked down; now he raised his eyes inquiringly. Will met his gaze directly and said—
“I suppose you knew my mother was alive, and knew where she could be found.”

Bulstrode recoiled. His face and hands visibly trembled. He had been entirely unprepared for this response to his offer, or for being pressed into revealing more than he had decided was necessary. At that moment, however, he dared not lie. Suddenly the ground on which he had stood with some confidence felt uncertain.

“I won’t deny that your guess is correct,” he answered unsteadily. “And I wish to make amends to you, as the only person still living who suffered a loss through me. I hope you understand my purpose, Mr. Ladislaw. It concerns claims higher than human ones and, as I’ve already said, is wholly independent of any legal obligation. I am prepared to reduce my own resources and my family’s expectations by committing myself to pay you five hundred pounds a year for as long as I live, and to leave you a corresponding sum of capital at my death. Indeed, I would do more if some worthy undertaking of yours clearly required it.” Mr. Bulstrode had moved on to these details in the expectation that they would make a powerful impression on Ladislaw and absorb his other feelings into grateful acceptance.
But Will looked utterly stubborn, his lower lip thrust out and his fingers in his side pockets. The offer had not moved him at all. He said firmly—
“Before I answer your proposal, Mr. Bulstrode, I must ask you a question or two. Were you involved in the business that originally produced this fortune?”
“Raffles has told him,” Mr. Bulstrode thought. How could he refuse to answer when his own voluntary disclosure had prompted the question? He said, “Yes.”
“And was that business thoroughly dishonorable, or wasn’t it? If its nature had become public, might the people involved have been classed with thieves and convicts?”
A cutting bitterness filled Will’s voice. He wanted to put the question as starkly as possible.

Bulstrode flushed with anger he could not suppress. He had prepared himself for a scene of self-humiliation, but his fierce pride and habit of authority overcame repentance and even fear when the young man he intended to benefit turned on him like a judge.
“The business existed before my involvement, sir. Nor is it your place to conduct an inquiry of that sort.” His voice remained low, but his answer came with sharp defiance.

“Yes, it is,” Will said, springing up again, hat in hand. “It is very much my place to ask when I have to decide whether to deal with you and accept your money. My good name matters to me. It matters that there should be no stain on my birth or my connections. Now I find there is a stain I can do nothing about. My mother felt it and tried to keep as far from it as she could. I shall do the same. Keep your ill-gotten money. If I had a fortune of my own, I’d gladly give it to anyone who could prove that what you’ve told me is untrue. The one thing I can thank you for is keeping the money until now, when I’m able to refuse it. Whether a man is a gentleman ought to depend on the man himself. Good night, sir.”

Bulstrode was about to reply, but Will had left the room with determined speed. A moment later the front door closed behind him. His furious rebellion against this inherited stain, forced upon his knowledge, was too strong for him to consider just then whether he had treated Bulstrode too harshly. Perhaps he had shown an arrogant lack of mercy to a man of sixty trying to put things right after time had made the attempt futile.

No outside listener could have fully understood the force of Will’s rejection or the bitterness of his language. Only he knew how immediately everything touching his sense of personal dignity affected his relationship with Dorothea and his feelings about Mr. Casaubon’s treatment of him. Among the impulses that drove him to fling Bulstrode’s offer back was the knowledge that he could never have told Dorothea he had accepted it.

After Will had gone, Bulstrode suffered a violent reaction and wept like a woman. Never before had a man of any higher standing than Raffles expressed open contempt for him. That contempt coursed through him like poison, leaving him unable to feel any consolation. Yet he had to stop even the relief of weeping. His wife and daughters soon returned from hearing a missionary to the East. They were full of regret that Papa had not heard for himself the interesting things they tried to repeat.
Perhaps, among all his hidden thoughts, the one that offered most comfort was that Will Ladislaw, at least, was unlikely to tell anyone what had happened that evening.
